papers.title: PP2A-B55α Terminates Mitophagy by Selectively Dephosphorylating Parkin via a Non-Canonical Interface
papers.summary: This paper identifies PP2A-B55α as the phosphatase that shuts down mitophagy by removing phosphate groups from Parkin, a key regulator of damaged mitochondria clearance. The enzyme binds Parkin through an unusual, non-standard interaction surface rather than the typical PP2A substrate-binding mode. This selective dephosphorylation acts as an 'off-switch' that resets Parkin after mitophagy has been activated, allowing the cycle to terminate properly.
papers.why: Understanding how mitophagy is terminated via Parkin dephosphorylation provides mechanistic insight directly relevant to studying mitophagy dysregulation in neurons, which is central to this PhD project.

papers.title: Variable penetrance of schizophrenia in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with impaired, but reversible, neuronal mitophagy
papers.summary: This study investigates why only some people with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome develop schizophrenia, focusing on neuronal mitophagy (the process of clearing damaged mitochondria). The researchers found that impaired mitophagy in neurons is linked to schizophrenia risk in this genetic condition. Importantly, this impairment appears reversible, suggesting a potential therapeutic target.
papers.why: This directly connects to the core focus on neuronal mitophagy and its link to psychiatric disease, offering mechanistic insight relevant to broader studies of mitochondrial quality control in brain cells.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitophagy flux assays or mitochondrial clearance markers comparing schizophrenia-penetrant vs non-penetrant 22q11.2 deletion carriers would be most informative.

papers.title: DEGS1 Loss Disrupts Autophagy, Lysosomal and Mitochondrial Function in Non-Neuronal Human HAP1 Cells and Neurite Morphology in Primary Neurons.
papers.summary: This study examines what happens when a gene called DEGS1, which is involved in making certain lipids, is lost in human HAP1 cells and primary neurons. The researchers found that losing DEGS1 disrupts autophagy (the cell's waste-clearing system), damages lysosomes, and impairs mitochondrial function in non-neuronal cells. In primary neurons, this same gene loss also caused abnormal changes in neurite shape and structure.
papers.why: Since the PhD project focuses on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons, this paper's findings on how a single gene loss disrupts autophagic and mitochondrial pathways while altering neuronal morphology provides direct mechanistic insight relevant to the core research questions.

papers.title: Multi-omics, spatial omics and artificial intelligence in chronic diseases: current applications and future directions.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how multi-omics, spatial omics, and artificial intelligence are being combined to study chronic diseases. It covers current methods for integrating molecular data across different biological layers with spatial information from tissues. The paper also discusses future directions for how these technologies could improve disease understanding and diagnosis.
papers.why: This broad review could offer useful context and methodological inspiration for integrating spatial transcriptomics, spatial metabolomics, and AI-driven analysis in studying mitophagy and autophagy in neurons and interneurons.

papers.title: Metformin regulates astrocyte autophagy via the AMPK/mTOR pathway to improve glutamate homeostasis and prevent cognitive impairment induced by cerebral ischemia-reperfusion
papers.summary: This study looks at how the drug metformin affects autophagy in astrocytes (support cells in the brain) after a stroke-like injury caused by cerebral ischemia-reperfusion. It finds that metformin works through the AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway, a key cellular energy-sensing route that controls autophagy. By boosting this autophagy process, metformin helps restore normal glutamate levels and reduces cognitive impairment following the injury.
papers.why: Although focused on astrocytes rather than neurons, this paper offers relevant mechanistic insight into AMPK/mTOR-regulated autophagy in the brain, which is directly transferable to understanding mitophagy/autophagy regulation in neurons and interneurons under metabolic or ischemic stress.

papers.title: Metformin regulates astrocyte autophagy via the AMPK/mTOR pathway to improve glutamate homeostasis and prevent cognitive impairment induced by cerebral ischemia-reperfusion.
papers.summary: This paper shows that metformin, a common diabetes drug, activates autophagy in astrocytes through the AMPK/mTOR signaling pathway. This autophagy activation helps astrocytes better regulate glutamate levels in the brain after a stroke-like injury (ischemia-reperfusion). As a result, treated animals show improved cognitive function, suggesting metformin could protect the brain by enhancing cellular cleanup processes in support cells.
papers.why: While this focuses on astrocytes rather than neurons, it offers valuable comparative insight into AMPK/mTOR-regulated autophagy mechanisms that may parallel or interact with mitophagy/autophagy pathways in neurons and interneurons under metabolic or ischemic stress.

papers.title: A Single-Capillary Open Microfluidic Probe for Robust and Versatile Spatial Multi-Omics Using Ambient Mass Spectrometry Imaging.
papers.summary: This paper introduces a new open microfluidic probe that uses a single capillary to collect molecules directly from tissue surfaces for analysis by ambient mass spectrometry imaging. The design aims to make spatial multi-omics measurements, like mapping lipids, metabolites, or other molecules across a tissue slice, more robust and easier to use than previous multi-channel probes. This could broaden access to spatial 'omics' mapping techniques for various tissue types without needing complex instrumentation.
papers.why: This probe technology could be adapted for spatial metabolomics of brain tissue, potentially enabling detection of metabolic signatures linked to mitophagy or perineuronal net composition around interneurons at fine spatial resolution.

papers.title: Multiplexed targeted iprm-PASEF assays for MALDI mass spectrometry imaging of lipids, NAD<sup>+</sup>, and related metabolites in CD38 knockout mice.
papers.summary: This paper describes a new mass spectrometry imaging method that can simultaneously detect many lipids, NAD+, and related metabolites directly in tissue sections with high spatial precision. The technique uses targeted iprm-PASEF assays combined with MALDI imaging to achieve multiplexed detection with better sensitivity and specificity than standard approaches. They apply this method to CD38 knockout mice, a model used to study NAD+ metabolism, to map how loss of this enzyme changes the spatial distribution of these molecules in tissue.
papers.why: This method offers a powerful approach for spatial metabolomics of NAD+ and lipid pathways in brain tissue, which could help link mitochondrial/metabolic states to mitophagy processes in neurons and interneurons.
